verify_runs.tail:
Bone-in and skin-on sardines and salmon. The bones soften completely. 
     The list should read fish, oil or water, salt. Anything longer is a sauce. 
     Good oil-packed tins are worth using in the dish rather than draining. 
     Skipjack, labeled ‘light’, sits lower on the mercury range than albacore, labeled ‘white’. 
     Skipjack, labeled ‘light’, is lower-mercury than albacore, labeled ‘white’. 
     An epoxy made with BPA lines many food cans. Fresh or frozen fish comes without a can lining. 
     Choose a can that says BPA-free on its label over a can that says nothing. 
     Packed in vegetable oil 
     Nearly always a seed oil blend. The tin will not name which. 
     Packed in olive oil 
     Check it says olive oil, not ‘olive oil blend’. 
     Skinless, boneless 
     Both removed. Convenient, and it takes out the part that makes a whole small fish worth eating. 
     The pack medium is on the list, and preferring olive oil or water is the standard laid over it. 
     ‘’ speaks to dolphins only. Seafood Watch says it does not mean the tuna is sustainable. The terms that do are FAD-free, free school or school-caught. They mean purse seines used without a floating device. That device draws in juvenile fish, sharks and other bycatch. 
     ‘Light’ tuna is skipjack, ‘white’ is albacore, and ‘ahi’ is usually yellowfin but may be bigeye. 
     BPA-free is a claim from the maker. EWG found that makers define it as they wish. In EWG’s survey, makers that dropped BPA did not disclose their replacement lining. 
     Read the pack medium: olive oil or water, not unnamed ‘vegetable oil’. 
     The list should read fish, oil or water, salt; bones and skin left in. 
     On tuna, look for FAD-free or school-caught; ‘’ covers dolphins only. 
     Tins differ almost entirely in pack medium and what else went in. ‘Vegetable oil’ is nearly always a seed oil blend, and the tin will not name which. Bone-in sardines and salmon keep the whole small fish, and the bones soften completely. Good olive-oil tins are worth using in the dish. ‘Light’ tuna is skipjack, lower in mercury than ‘white’ albacore; ‘ahi’ is usually yellowfin.
